sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Pseudoexfoliation (PXF) is a systemic microfibrillopathy characterized by the production and progressive accumulation of an abnormal fibrillar material in ocular tissues and visceral organs. It involves a mutation in the LOXL1 gene. In the eye, this proteinaceous material deposits on the lens capsule, iris, and zonules, leading to zonular fragility and basement membrane dysfunction.

sections.title: The PXF Ocular Examination
content: Classic Three-Zone Lens Pattern: Central disc, peripheral granular zone, and clear intermediate zone.
Sampaolesi Line: Pigment deposition anterior to Schwalbe's line on gonioscopy.
Pupillary 'Moth-eaten' Atrophy: Transillumination defects at the sphincter.
Phacodonesis: Visible wobbling of the lens during rapid eye movements (indicates severe zonular loss).
Iridodonesis: Shaking of the iris upon eye movement due to lack of lens support.
Asymmetric Anterior Chamber Depth: May suggest subluxation or zonular laxity.

sections.title: Preoperative Red Flags
content: Frank Phacodonesis or Subluxation
History of ocular trauma (compounds PXF fragility)
Poor pupillary response to maximum mydriatics (< 4mm)
Angle closure or Very Shallow AC depth
Vitreous in the anterior chamber (spontaneous vitreous prolapse)

sections.title: Surgical Strategy: Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Maximizing Mydriasis - Use intracameral phenylephrine/lidocaine or mechanical dilators.
Step 2: Capsulorhexis (CCC) - Larger CCC (5.5mm-6.0mm) is safer to reduce later capsular phimosis.
Step 3: Hydrodissection - Perform 'Cortical Cleaving' hydrodissection to minimize zonular stress during rotation.
Step 4: Phacoemulsification - Use 'Slow Motion' settings; keep the nucleus central; avoid 'Push-Pull' maneuvers.
Step 5: CTR Insertion - Insert as LATE as possible (after cortex removal) unless necessary for stability during phaco.
Step 6: Cortex Removal - Use tangential stripping rather than radial pulling to protect remaining zonules.

sections.title: Postoperative Counseling & Warnings
content: Risk of Early IOP Spikes: PXF patients have compromised trabecular meshwork; monitor pressure 2-4 hours post-op.
Late IOL Dislocation: Explain that the entire 'bag' can dislocate years later, even if the surgery was perfect.
Chronic Inflammation: Higher risk of postoperative uveitis and fibrinous reactions.
Capsular Phimosis: The capsulorhexis opening may shrink over time; YAG laser capsulotomy may be needed.
Corneal Endothelial Fragility: PXF is associated with lower cell counts; recovery may be slower.

sections.title: Surgical Complication Management
content: Sudden deepening of AC: Suspect Posterior Capsule Rupture (PCR).
Lens Tilt during Phaco: Indicates focal zonular dialysis.
Vitreous Prolapse: Perform early bimanual anterior vitrectomy; do NOT use sponge and scissors.
Dropped Nucleus: Do not chase! Level the eye and refer to a vitreoretinal surgeon.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Success
content: Use highly dispersive OVD (e.g., Viscoat) to protect the endothelium.
Try to avoid IOLs with high-angulation haptics if zonules are weak.
Always check for a Sampaolesi line in any 'glaucoma suspect'.
If the bag is extremely loose, consider 3-piece IOL in the sulcus with optic capture.

sections.title: Landmark Evidence
sections.content: The SCORPIO Study and various Nordic registries have highlighted that PXF is the leading identifiable cause of open-angle glaucoma and spontaneous IOL-capsular bag dislocation. Recent data suggests that early cataract intervention might be safer than waiting for the cataract to become 'hypermature' and zonules to further degrade.
